notes.meaning: Caesarea was a major seaside city that served as the Roman government center in Judea. A centurion was an officer in the Roman army who commanded about one hundred soldiers. Cornelius led a group within the Italian Regiment, an army unit made up of Roman citizens from Italy.

Cornelius and his whole family worshipped the God of Israel, even though they were Gentiles who had not fully joined the Jewish religion. He showed his faith by giving money generously to needy Jewish people and by praying to God continually. His life showed true reverence toward God and practical love for his neighbors.

The ninth hour was three o'clock in the afternoon, which was a regular time for Jewish afternoon prayer. While praying in broad daylight, Cornelius clearly saw an angel sent from God. The angel called him by name to show that God knew him personally and had a direct message for him.

Cornelius looked at the angel and felt sudden fear and awe. The angel told him that God had noticed his prayers and his gifts to the poor. In the Old Testament, gifts burned on the altar were called a memorial offering, and God received the good deeds of Cornelius like a pleasing sacrifice.

differ.view: Cornelius was already born again by the Holy Spirit and had saving faith like Old Testament believers, which is why God accepted his prayers.
Cornelius did not yet have saving faith in Christ, but God graciously accepted his sincere seeking through prayer and charity.

notes.meaning: The angel told Cornelius to send messengers south down the coast to the city of Joppa. They were to find a man named Simon, who was also known as Peter. God used an angel to give directions, but He chose a human preacher to share the good news of salvation.

Peter was staying as a guest in the home of another Simon, who worked as a tanner preparing animal hides. Tanners often lived by the seashore outside the main town because their work created bad smells and made them ritually unclean to strict Jews. The angel gave exact directions so the messengers could find the right house without trouble.

As soon as the angel left, Cornelius obeyed the heavenly message without delay. He called two of his household servants and a trusted soldier who also feared the true God. The faith and character of Cornelius had clearly spread to the people who worked under him.

Cornelius explained everything that had happened to his servants and the soldier. Sharing the vision helped them understand the holy purpose of their trip and prepare to explain it clearly to Peter. Then he sent them off on the journey to Joppa.

The messengers traveled about thirty miles and were coming near Joppa around noon the next day. At that same hour, Peter went up onto the flat roof of the house to pray. God was guiding the actions of both men miles apart so they would meet at the perfect moment.

While on the roof, Peter became very hungry as the family below was preparing lunch. While he waited, God placed him into a trance, which was a special state where ordinary senses paused so he could receive a direct vision. God used Peter's physical hunger to teach him an important spiritual truth.

In the vision, Peter saw the sky open and an object like a giant linen sheet come down to the ground. It was held securely by its four corners as it was lowered from heaven. The open sky showed that the lesson Peter was about to receive came straight from God.

Inside the sheet was a wide mixture of all kinds of animals, reptiles, and birds. Under the law of Moses, God had forbidden Jews from eating certain unclean animals like pigs or reptiles. Seeing all these creatures grouped together without any separation startled Peter's Jewish upbringing.

A heavenly voice told Peter to stand up, kill any of the animals, and eat them. This was a direct test of the old dietary rules that separated Jewish people from other nations. God was preparing Peter to accept a major change in how believers were to relate to Gentiles.

Peter refused the command, saying he had never eaten anything common or unclean in his entire life. He had carefully kept the food laws of the Old Testament since childhood. Even though he recognized the Lord's voice, his lifelong religious habits made him pull back in alarm.

The voice spoke again, telling Peter not to call unholy what God Himself had cleansed. God has the supreme authority to declare what is clean and proper. While the vision used animals, it was really about people, teaching that Gentiles were no longer to be viewed as unclean outsiders.

This whole exchange happened three times before the sheet was pulled back up into heaven. The repetition ensured that Peter could not mistake the message or treat it as an accident. God made the lesson completely certain before the vision ended.

Peter came out of the trance and felt completely puzzled about what the vision meant. While he was turning the matter over in his mind, the messengers sent by Cornelius arrived at the gate outside. God used this real-world event to provide the key that unlocked the meaning of the vision.

The visitors stood at the gate and called out into the courtyard. They asked politely whether Simon Peter was staying there as a guest. Their question matched the exact name and place the angel had given to Cornelius.

While Peter was still up on the roof thinking hard about the vision, the Holy Spirit spoke clearly to his inner heart. The Spirit told him that three men were downstairs looking for him. This direct guidance showed that God was directing every step of the visit.

The Holy Spirit told Peter to go downstairs immediately and travel with the visitors without any hesitation. Strict Jews usually avoided traveling with Gentiles or entering their homes. The Spirit commanded Peter to set aside those doubts because God Himself had sent the men.
Peter obeyed the Spirit, went downstairs to the entrance, and met the men. He introduced himself as the person they were seeking. Then he asked them why they had come, ready to hear their story.

The messengers explained that Cornelius the centurion was an upright, God-fearing man who was well respected by the Jewish community. They told Peter that an angel had ordered Cornelius to invite him over so he could hear God's message. Their words showed Peter why the Spirit had told him to go.

Peter welcomed the Gentile travelers into the house and gave them lodging for the night, breaking old Jewish social rules. The next morning, Peter left with them, accompanied by six Jewish believers from Joppa. These companions went along to serve as witnesses of whatever God was about to do among the Gentiles.

On the second day of their journey, Peter and his companions arrived in Caesarea. Cornelius was eagerly waiting for them and had gathered his relatives and close friends in his house. He wanted everyone he cared about to hear the good news from God alongside him.
